p: The Greek Old Testament adds that Orpah "went back to her people."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law
readings.plain: And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law,

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus)
readings.orig: καὶ κατεφίλησεν Ορφα τὴν πενθερὰν αὐτῆς καὶ ἐπέστρεψεν εἰς τὸν λαὸν αὐτῆς
readings.en: and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned to her people
readings.plain: And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and went back to her people,

why: The Hebrew is shorter, and the Greek addition looks like a translator spelling out what Naomi says in the next verse (1:15). Translators usually prefer the shorter reading when a longer one can be explained as a helpful addition.
b: The Septuagint also says that Ruth "followed" Naomi, a looser rendering of "clung." Neither change alters the story: 1:15 says plainly that Orpah went back.

a: the LORD has testified against me
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read "testified against me" or "humbled me." The Greek has "humbled me."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (the vowels added by Jewish scribes); Targum; KJV, BSB
readings.en: the LORD has testified against me
readings.plain: the LORD has testified against me

readings.w: Septuagint; Syriac Peshitta; Latin Vulgate (humiliavit me); followed by the RSV, NRSV and NIV
readings.orig: καὶ κύριος ἐταπείνωσέν με (Hebrew vowels read as עִנָּה בִי)
readings.en: the LORD has humbled me
readings.plain: the LORD has humbled me

why: The letters are the same; only the vowels differ, and vowels were not written in the earliest Hebrew. The Masoretic reading "answered against me" is a legal phrase for testifying against someone (Exodus 20:16; 1 Samuel 12:3), and it fits Naomi's courtroom picture of God as her accuser. "Humbled" (or "afflicted") is also possible and matches the next line. Both are old; the Plain English keeps the Hebrew tradition.

p: The written Hebrew says "someone known"; the reading tradition says "relative."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading said aloud); KJV "kinsman"
readings.en: a relative
readings.plain: a relative

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written letters)
readings.en: someone known, an acquaintance
readings.plain: an acquaintance

why: The scribes wrote one word and told readers to say another. The reading tradition, moda', matches the related word in 3:2 ("our relative"). The written form could also mean "close friend" (2 Kings 10:11; Psalm 55:13), so the difference is small.
b: In a Ketiv/Qere the consonants in the scroll (Ketiv, "what is written") were never changed, but a note in the margin told the reader what to say (Qere, "what is read"). Ruth has about a dozen of these.

a: She has sat in the shelter only a short while.
t: A hard verse in every version
p: The Hebrew is unclear, literally "this her sitting the house a little." The Greek reads quite differently.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: this her sitting (in) the house (is) a little
readings.plain: She has sat in the shelter only a short while.

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: ἀπὸ πρωίθεν καὶ ἕως ἑσπέρας, οὐ κατέπαυσεν ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ μικρόν
readings.en: from morning until evening; she has not rested in the field even a little
readings.plain: She has not rested in the field even a little.

why: The Hebrew is terse and probably damaged, but it can be understood as a short break "in the house," meaning a field shelter. The Greek may come from a different Hebrew text or may be a translator's guess at the same hard words. Both agree that Ruth worked hard all morning.
b: The Septuagint also has "from morning until evening" where the Hebrew has "from the morning until now." The Latin Vulgate goes its own way: ne ad momentum quidem domum reversa est, "not even for a moment has she gone home." Some scholars correct the Hebrew in other ways, for example "she has not rested even a little." There is no agreement, so the Plain English keeps the received text.

p: The written Hebrew has "your cloak" (singular); the reading tradition says "your clothes."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written letters)
readings.en: your cloak
readings.plain: put your cloak on

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading said aloud); KJV "raiment," BSB "best clothes"
readings.en: your garments
readings.plain: put your clothes on

why: The singular simlah is the outer wrap, the garment Ruth would wear against the night cold. Either reading works. The Plain English follows the written text here because it gives a clearer picture; "best clothes" in some versions is an interpretation of the plural.

a: and go down to the threshing floor
t: "You go down" or "I will go down"?
p: The written Hebrew looks like "I will go down," but it is probably an old spelling of "you will go down."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading said aloud); all major translations
readings.en: and you will go down
readings.plain: and go down to the threshing floor

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written letters)
readings.en: and I will go down (or an old form of "you will go down")
readings.plain: and I will go down to the threshing floor

why: The ending -ti was an old way of writing "you" when speaking to a woman, found in other places too (compare 3:4 and Jeremiah 2:20). So the Ketiv probably means the same as the Qere. A midrash took the written form literally: Naomi said, "My merit will go down with you."

t: "Tell me": a word read but not written
p: The words "to me" are read aloud in the synagogue but are missing from the written Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (read aloud; known as "read but not written"); KJV, BSB
readings.en: all that you say to me
readings.plain: everything you tell me

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written letters)
readings.en: all that you say
readings.plain: everything you say

why: The meaning hardly changes. The Masoretes marked a few places where a word should be read even though it is not in the scroll; Ruth 3:5 and 3:17 are two of them. The reading tradition is followed.

a: Then he went into the town.
t: Who went into town, Boaz or Ruth?
p: The Hebrew says "he went," so Boaz went to the gate. Some manuscripts, the KJV, ESV and NASB say "she went."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum (which names Boaz); NIV, NRSV, BSB
readings.en: and he went into the city
readings.plain: Then he went into the town.

readings.w: Some medieval Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac Peshitta and the Latin Vulgate (ingressa est civitatem); KJV, ESV, NASB
readings.en: and she went into the city
readings.plain: Then she went into the town.

why: "He went" is the harder reading, since the next verse is about Ruth arriving home, and a scribe was more likely to change "he" to "she" to smooth the story than the reverse. It also sets up 4:1: Boaz goes straight to the town gate.
b: The Qumran fragment 2QRuth-b covers 3:13–18, but its reading at this word has not been checked for this entry. Modern versions are divided, usually with a footnote.

t: Another word read but not written
p: As in 3:5, the words "to me" are read aloud but missing from the written text.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (read aloud); KJV, BSB
readings.en: for he said to me
readings.plain: he said to me

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (the written letters)
readings.en: for he said
readings.plain: he said

why: The meaning is the same either way. The reading tradition is followed.

a: But if you will not redeem it
p: The standard Hebrew text says "if he will not redeem." Other witnesses and nearly all translations say "you."

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, Targum; KJV, BSB and most versions
readings.en: but if you will not redeem
readings.plain: But if you will not redeem it

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: but if he will not redeem
readings.plain: But if he will not redeem it

why: Boaz is speaking to the man face to face, so "you" fits. The Hebrew letters for "he" and "you" here differ by only one letter, and the two do not look alike, so the slip was probably not visual: a scribe may have been influenced by speaking about the redeemer in the third person. A few scholars defend the Masoretic "he" as Boaz turning aside to address the elders for a moment. The Qumran fragment 2QRuth-a contains parts of 4:3–4, but its reading at this word has not been checked for this entry.

a: you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife,
p: Two small Hebrew differences change who acquires Ruth, and whether Ruth is a seller or a wife.

readings.w: A one-letter correction (וְאֵת, 'and also') supported by the Latin Vulgate, with the Qere 'you acquire'; most modern versions
readings.en: and also Ruth... you acquire
readings.plain: you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife,

readings.w: Masoretic Text with the Qere 'you acquire' (the KJV's reading)
readings.en: and from Ruth... you acquire
readings.plain: you also buy it from Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife,

readings.w: Septuagint, the oldest witness here
readings.orig: καὶ παρὰ Ρουθ τῆς Μωαβίτιδος γυναικὸς τοῦ τεθνηκότος, καὶ αὐτὴν κτήσασθαί σε δεῖ
readings.en: and from Ruth the Moabite, wife of the dead man, and you must also acquire her
readings.plain: and from Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife, you must also acquire her

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv 'I acquire', usually with the same one-letter correction; argued by D. R. G. Beattie and others
readings.en: and Ruth... I acquire
readings.plain: I also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife,

why: Verse 4:10 says Boaz "acquired" Ruth as his wife, using the same verb, so most scholars read 4:5 the same way: buying the field brings the duty of marrying Ruth. That needs only one letter changed (ume'et "and from" to ve'et "and also"). The KJV keeps the Masoretic "from Ruth," making Ruth a co-seller of the land, which is hard to fit with 4:9. The written form "I acquire" would mean Boaz is announcing his own marriage to Ruth before the man decides, so that the land would go to Ruth's future son either way (the view of D. R. G. Beattie and some others).
b: The verse turns on two things: the little word before Ruth's name, and the Ketiv/Qere on the verb. The Septuagint keeps both sides: it follows the Hebrew "from Ruth" and the spoken "you acquire," and adds "her" as the object, so the Greek translator seems to have read the consonants we have and smoothed the sense. The surviving Qumran fragment (2QRuth-a, 4:3–4) does not include this verse. Every option has defenders, and translators should be honest that the text is uncertain.

a: and he pulled off his sandal.
t: Who gave the sandal to whom?
p: The Greek adds "and gave it to him," making clear that the redeemer gave his sandal to Boaz.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: and he drew off his sandal
readings.plain: and he pulled off his sandal.

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: Κτῆσαι σεαυτῷ τὴν ἀγχιστείαν μου ... καὶ ὑπελύσατο τὸ ὑπόδημα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ
readings.en: Acquire for yourself my right of redemption... and he took off his sandal and gave it to him
readings.plain: and he pulled off his sandal and gave it to him.

why: The shorter Hebrew is followed. The Greek additions, "my right of redemption" in the speech and "and gave it to him" at the end, spell out what 4:6–7 already explain. Who gave the object to whom was debated in antiquity: the Targum has Boaz take off his right-hand glove, reflecting a later custom of acquisition by symbolic exchange, and the Talmud (Bava Metzia 47a) records Rav and Levi disputing whether Boaz or the redeemer gave it.

a: May you do worthy things in Ephrathah and make a name in Bethlehem.
p: In the Greek, the worthy deeds belong to Rachel and Leah, not to Boaz, and the elders speak separately.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: and do worth in Ephrathah and proclaim a name in Bethlehem
readings.plain: May you do worthy things in Ephrathah and make a name in Bethlehem.

readings.w: Septuagint
readings.orig: καὶ ἐποίησαν δύναμιν ἐν Εφραθα, καὶ ἔσται ὄνομα ἐν Βαιθλεεμ
readings.en: and they did valiantly in Ephratha, and there shall be a name in Bethlehem
readings.plain: They did worthy things in Ephrathah, and there will be a name in Bethlehem.

why: The Hebrew is a blessing addressed to Boaz, which fits the following verse ("may your house be like the house of Perez"). The Greek turns it into a statement about Rachel and Leah and also divides the speakers: all the people say "Witnesses," and the elders give the blessing. The Masoretic Text is followed as the harder, more personal reading.
b: Chayil, "worth," appears for the third time here: Boaz is a man of chayil (2:1), Ruth a woman of chayil (3:11), and now the town prays that their household will "do chayil," which probably includes having children. "Make a name" means to become famous, and also to have a name carried on.

p: The Hebrew spells the name Salmah in 4:20 and Salmon in 4:21. They are the same man.

readings.w: Masoretic Text in 4:21; Matthew 1:4–5 (Greek Salmōn); most English versions
readings.en: Salmon
readings.plain: Salmon

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) in 4:20; compare 1 Chronicles 2:11, Salma
readings.en: Salmah
readings.plain: Salmah

why: Both forms name the same person, one verse apart, so the Plain English uses one spelling to avoid confusion. Names in genealogies often have more than one form (compare Ram and Aram, Matthew 1:3–4).
